The '''2016–17 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team''' represented [[Georgetown University]] in the [[2016–17 NCAA Division I men's basketball season]]. The Hoyas, led by 13th-year head coach [[John Thompson III]], played their home games at the [[Capital One Arena|Verizon Center]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], and were members of the [[Big East Conference]].

The season saw the return of [[Jonathan Wallace]], the Hoyas′ standout [[point guard]] from [[2004–05 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2004]] to [[2007–08 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2008]], to the basketball program as a special assistant after eight seasons playing professional basketball in the [[NBA Summer League]], the [[National Basketball Association]] Developmental League, [[Belgium]], [[Germany]], and [[Angola]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.guhoyas.com/sports/m-baskbl/spec-rel/082416aaa.html |title=guhoyas.com "Former Hoya Jonathan Wallace Joins Men's Basketball Staff at Georgetown," August 24, 2016. |access-date=March 19, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170319112157/http://www.guhoyas.com/sports/m-baskbl/spec-rel/082416aaa.html |archive-date=March 19, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The Hoyas finished the season at 14–18, 5–13 in [[2016–17 Big East Conference men's basketball season|Big East play]], to finish in ninth place in the conference. As the No. 9 seed in the [[2017 Big East men's basketball tournament|Big East tournament]], they lost in the first round to [[2016–17 St. John's Red Storm men's basketball team|St. John's]]. Georgetown finished the season with a losing record for the second straight year, the first time that had happened since the [[1971–72 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1972]] and [[1972–73 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1973]] seasons, and without an invitation to a postseason tournament in consecutive years for the first time since 1972 and 1973.

On March 23, 2017, Georgetown officials announced that John Thompson III had been [[dismissal (employment)|fired]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/story/_/id/18984268/georgetown-hoyas-parting-ways-john-thompson-iii|title=Hoyas dismiss coach John Thompson III after 13 seasons|work=[[ESPN]]|author=Jeff Goodman and Jeff Borzello|date=2017-03-23|access-date=2017-03-23}}</ref><ref name="santamariahoffman20170324"/><ref>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown fires head coach John Thompson III after 13 years|url=https://www.si.com/college/2017/03/23/georgetown-hoyas-john-thompson-iii-coach-fired-resigns|access-date=2022-10-16|date=March 23, 2017|website=Sports Illustrated|language=en-us}}</ref> On April 2, it was reported that [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame|Basketball Hall of Famer]] and Georgetown alumnus [[Patrick Ewing]] would replace Thompson as head coach.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/ncaab/bigeast/2017/04/03/patrick-ewing-georgetown-coach/99988542/|title=Patrick Ewing hired as coach of Georgetown|work=USA TODAY|access-date=2017-04-03|language=en}}</ref>

==Previous season==
The [[2015–16 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|Hoyas]] finished the [[2015–16 NCAA Division I men's basketball season|2015–16 season]] 15–18, 7–11 in [[2015–16 Big East Conference men's basketball season|Big East play]] to finish in eighth place. They defeated [[2015–16 DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball team|DePaul]] in the first round of the [[2016 Big East men's basketball tournament|Big East tournament]] to advance to the quarterfinals where they lost to [[2015–16 Villanova Wildcats men's basketball team|Villanova]]. For the first time in John Thompson III's twelve years as head coach, the Hoyas did not make a postseason tournament.

==Season recap==

Georgetown had lost three players since the conclusion of [[2015–16 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|the previous season]]. Little-used [[Walk-on (sports)|walk-on]] senior [[Guard (basketball)|guard]] Riyan Williams – the son of Georgetown great [[Reggie Williams (basketball, born 1964)|Reggie Williams]] – had graduated with a year of college eligibility remaining and chose to transfer to [[NCAA Division II]] [[Goldey-Beacom College]] to play his final year of [[college basketball]], and sophomore [[Forward (basketball)|forward]] Paul White, the team's leading scorer off the bench during [[2014–15 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|his freshman year]] but limited by a hip injury to seven games during the 2015–2016 season, had transferred to [[Oregon Ducks men's basketball|Oregon]] at the end of August 2016. By far the team's biggest loss, however, was guard [[D'Vauntes Smith-Rivera]], whose graduation in 2016 left the Hoyas without their leading scorer of the past three seasons. Although a natural [[shooting guard]] who finished his college career as Georgetown's fifth-leading all-time scorer<ref name=santamaria20160310>{{Cite web|date=2016-03-11|title=Men's Basketball | Hoyas End Big East Tournament Run With 81-67 Loss to Wildcats|url=https://thehoya.com/mens-basketball-hoyas-end-big-east-tournament-run-with-81-67-loss-to-wildcats/|access-date=2022-10-16|language=en-US}}</ref> and with more three-pointers made than any previous Hoya,<ref name=santamaria20160310/> Smith-Rivera had also served as the team's [[point guard]] for the past two seasons, and the team keenly felt the loss of both his scoring ability and his in-game leadership.

At forward, senior Reggie Cameron, juniors [[Isaac Copeland]], [[Trey Mourning]], and [[L. J. Peak]], and sophomores [[Marcus Derrickson]] and Kaleb Johnson all returned for 2016–2017. Junior guard Tre Campbell and sophomore [[Center (basketball)|center]] Jesse Govan also came back for another season. Forward Akoy Agau, who had transferred from [[Louisville Cardinals men's basketball|Louisville]] in January 2015 and had planned to begin play for Georgetown in January 2016 after sitting out the two full semesters the [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] mandated for transferring players, had missed the entire 2015–2016 season while recovering from knee surgery,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown's Akoy Agau suffers season-ending injury|url=https://www.nbcsports.com/washington/georgetown-hoyas/georgetowns-akoy-agau-suffers-season-ending-injury|access-date=2022-10-16|website=RSN|language=en}}</ref> but he finally would make his Georgetown debut in 2016–2017 as a [[Redshirt (sports)|redshirt]] junior. A surprise returnee from the previous season was fifth-year senior center Bradley Hayes; he was due to graduate in 2016, and virtually everyone, including Hayes himself, believed as the 2015–2016 season came to an end that his college career was over. However, John Thompson III applied for an NCAA waiver that would allow Hayes to return for a fifth year as a redshirt senior in 2016–2017<ref name=santamaria20160429>{{Cite web|date=2016-04-29|title=Men's Basketball | Hayes Returns for 5th Year|url=https://thehoya.com/mens-basketball-2/|access-date=2022-10-16|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=dauster20170118>{{Cite web|date=2017-01-19|title=Triumph over Tragedy: Bradley Hayes' long road ends as a Georgetown graduate|url=https://collegebasketball.nbcsports.com/2017/01/18/triumph-over-tragedy-bradley-hayes-long-road-ends-as-a-georgetown-graduate/|access-date=2022-10-16|website=College Basketball | NBC Sports|language=en-US}}</ref> because he had played in only nine games and for only 14 minutes during [[2012–13 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|his freshman year]] and had a semester to go to complete his degree.<ref name=dauster20170118/> The NCAA granted the waiver, provided that Hayes sat out the first four games of the 2016–2017 season.<ref name=dauster20170118/> The team's former student manager, junior guard Ra'Mond Hines, who had made the team for the first time as a walk-on late the previous season, also returned to the team for 2016–2017, again as a walk-on.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-03-10|title=Walk This Way: Ra'Mond Hines' two-week journey from Georgetown manager to the floor of MSG|url=https://georgetownvoice.com/2016/03/10/walk-this-way-ramond-hines-two-week-journey-from-georgetown-manager-to-the-floor-of-msg/|access-date=2022-10-16|website=The Georgetown Voice|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Ra'Mond Hines - Men's Basketball|url=https://guhoyas.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/ra-mond-hines/496|access-date=2022-10-16|website=Georgetown University Athletics|language=en}}</ref>

Two freshmen joined the team, guard Jagan Moseley and walk-on forward George Muresan, the son of former [[National Basketball Association]] center [[Gheorghe Muresan]]. Also arriving for the year were two upperclassmen. Guard Rodney Pryor had transferred from [[Robert Morris Colonials men's basketball|Robert Morris]] and was eligible to play for Georgetown immediately as a redshirt senior because he had graduated from Robert Morris the previous spring. Junior guard Jonathan Mulmore, a [[junior college]] transfer from [[Allegany College of Maryland]], also joined the team.

===Nonconference schedule===

Georgetown began its season by defeating [[2016–17 USC Upstate Spartans men's basketball team|South Carolina Upstate]] in a game at the Verizon Center in which the Hoyas started only one player (Isaac Copeland) who had started their final game of the previous season.<ref name=stevens20161112/> Georgetown displayed a very different style of play from that seen previously under John Thompson III, with frequent presses and more running,<ref name=stevens20161112/> and won 105–60.<ref name=stevens20161112/> It was Georgetown's greatest offensive output since the Hoyas scored 111 points against [[2010–11 Missouri Tigers men's basketball team|Missouri]] in an overtime victory on [[2010–11 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|November 30, 2010]],<ref name=stevens20161112/> the fifth time the Hoyas had scored 100 or more points in a game during John Thompson III's 13 seasons as head coach,<ref name=ap20161112>{{Cite web|title=South Carolina Upstate vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - November 12, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400918844|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and the third-highest scoring output of Thompson's tenure.<ref name=stevens20161112/> It was the highest-scoring season opener under Thompson,<ref name=stevens20161112/> the first 100-plus-point season opener for Georgetown since they beat [[NCAA Division III]] [[Marymount University|Marymount]] 108–47 to start the [[2001–02 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2001–2002 season]],<ref name=stevens20161112/> and the first time the Hoyas had scored 100 points or more in a season opener against an [[NCAA Division I]] opponent since defeating [[Colgate Raiders men's basketball|Colgate]] 106–57 to begin the [[1995–96 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1995–1996 season]].<ref name=stevens20161112/> Making his Hoya debut, Rodney Pryor sank a career-high six three-pointers on eight attempts from beyond the arc.<ref name=ap20161112/> and shot 13-of-16 (81.3 percent) from the field overall<ref name=ap20161112/> on the way to a 32-point game.<ref name=ap20161112/> Pryor scored 26 points in the first half alone,<ref name=ap20161112/> and the 68 points the Hoyas scored by halftime set a school record for first-half points,<ref name=ap20161112/> eclipsing the 57 points they scored in the first half against [[2008–09 Savannah State Tigers basketball team|Savannah State]] on [[2008–09 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|December 8, 2008]],<ref name=stevens20161112/> and it was the highest-scoring half for Georgetown in the 21st century to that point.<ref name=stevens20161112/> Overall, the Hoyas shot 66.7 percent from the field,<ref name=stevens20161112/> and L. J. Peak scored 14 points against the Spartans,<ref name=ap20161112/> Jesse Govan had 11,<ref name=boxscore20161112>{{Cite web|title=South Carolina Upstate vs. Georgetown - Box Score - November 12, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400918844|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Isaac Copeland scored 10,<ref name=boxscore20161112/> and Tre Campbell came off the bench to add 10.<ref name=boxscore20161112/>
[[File:Jessie Govan.jpg|thumb|Center [[Jessie Govan]] in action against [[2016–17 Maryland Terrapins men's basketball team|Maryland]] at the [[Capital One Arena|Verizon Center]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], on November 15, 2016.]]
Three days later, Georgetown took part in the annual [[Gavitt Tipoff Games]], a series of eight games per year between teams of the [[Big East Conference]] and [[Big Ten Conference]]. For the second straight year, Georgetown drew [[2016–17 Maryland Terrapins men's basketball team|Maryland]] as its Big Ten opponent, hosting the Terrapins at the Verizon Center – the first time the Hoyas had hosted the Terrapins since [[1993–94 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1993]].<ref name=ap20161115>{{Cite web|title=Maryland vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - November 15, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400915019|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> The Hoyas made 37 of their 42 free throws<ref name=ap20161115/> but blew a 68–59 lead with 2:21 remaining as Maryland went on a 17–7 scoring run the rest of the way to win the game, 76–75, defeating Georgetown for the second season in a row.<ref name=ap20161115/> Maryland's players stormed the court to celebrate the victory.<ref name=ap20161115/> Scoring 21 points, L. J. Peak<ref name=boxscore20161115>{{Cite web|title=Maryland vs. Georgetown - Box Score - November 15, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400915019|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> led a balanced Georgetown attack which also saw Rodney Pryor score 14 points,<ref name=boxscore20161115/> Isaac Copeland finish with a [[double-double]] (13 points and 13 rebounds),<ref name=boxscore20161115/> and Jesse Govan add 12 points.<ref name=boxscore20161115/>

Next up for the Hoyas was the [[Maui Invitational Tournament]]. Georgetown began the tournament by hosting a non-bracketed opening-round game against [[2016–17 Arkansas State Red Wolves men's basketball team|Arkansas State]] at [[McDonough Gymnasium]], the Hoyas′ first game on campus since the [[2014 National Invitation Tournament]]. The Hoyas shot only 3-for-18 (16.7 percent) from three-point range<ref name=ap20161117>{{Cite web|title=Arkansas State vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - November 17, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400915913|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and, despite Jesse Govan's 20 points,<ref name=ap20161117/> L. J. Peak's 18,<ref name=ap20161117/> and Isaac Copeland's 11,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Arkansas State vs. Georgetown - Box Score - November 17, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400915913|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> the Red Wolves led by double figures for much of the game<ref name=ap20161117/> and held off a 22-7 late-game Georgetown rally to upset the Hoyas 78–72.<ref name=ap20161117/> Thanks to the surprising loss, Georgetown opened its season with a 1–2 record for the second straight year.

Four days later, the Hoyas were in [[Hawaii]] at the [[Lahaina Civic Center]] in [[Lahaina, Hawaii|Lahaina]], [[Maui]], to open the bracketed championship round of the tournament with a quarterfinal match-up against their first ranked opponent of the year, No. 13 [[2016–17 Oregon Ducks men's basketball team|Oregon]]. The Ducks struggled against a strong Hoya defense and did not score a field goal for the first six minutes,<ref name=ap20161121>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Oregon - Game Recap - November 21, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400915516|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> shooting 7-for-29 (24.1 percent) from the field in the first half.<ref name=ap20161121/> Rodney Pryor, meanwhile, led Georgetown through Oregon's pressure defense during the half, and his buzzer-beating three-pointer gave the Hoyas a 38–21 halftime lead.<ref name=ap20161121/> In the second half, however, the Ducks′ pressure defense was far more effective, and it allowed them to force turnovers and make easy transition baskets.<ref name=ap20161121/> While Georgetown missed its first 12 shots of the second half,<ref name=ap20161121/> Oregon opened the half with a 22–4 scoring run that gave the Ducks a 43–42 lead.<ref name=ap20161121/> The Hoyas then staged a 10–2 scoring run of their own to pull out to a 52–45 lead with three minutes to play.<ref name=ap20161121/> Oregon responded with a late run and, with 3.8 seconds remaining, closed to a 63–61 deficit on a long three-pointer by junior forward [[Dillon Brooks]],<ref name=ap20161121/> but L. J. Peak hit two free throws with 2.7 seconds to play to secure a 65–61 upset Georgetown victory.<ref name=ap20161121/> Pryor had a double-double with 26 points and 10 rebounds,<ref name=ap20161121/> and Peak finished with 17 points.<ref name=ap20161121/> The Hoyas evened their record at 2–2, but had begun to show a tendency toward inconsistent play during their first four games, sometimes playing dominating basketball and then struggling mightily during other stretches of their games.<ref name=ap20161121/>

The Hoyas advanced to the semifinals the next day to meet another ranked opponent, No. 16 [[2016–17 Wisconsin Badgers men's basketball team|Wisconsin]], which had defeated [[2016–17 Tennessee Volunteers basketball team|Tennessee]] in the quarterfinals the previous day. The Hoyas never really found their shooting touch, but they held their own in the first half and Wisconsin clung to a 32–29 lead at halftime.<ref name=ap20161122>{{Cite web|title=Wisconsin vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - November 22, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400926704|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> During the second half, however, the Badgers opened with a scoring run that gave them a 44–34 lead,<ref name=ap20161122/> and by midway through the half led 53–39<ref name=ap20161122/> on their way to a 73–57 victory.<ref name=ap20161122/> During the game, Wisconsin shot only 5-for-22 (22.7 percent) from three-point range,<ref name=ap20161122/> but rebounding proved to be the game's decisive factor: Wisconsin had a 19–1 advantage in offensive rebounds<ref name=ap20161122/> and scored 20 second-chance points,<ref name=ap20161122/> and overall the Badgers outrebounded the Hoyas 50-21<ref name=ap20161122/> and outscored Georgetown 38–16 in the paint.<ref name=ap20161122/> The Hoyas′ poor performance on the boards prompted John Thompson III to observe during his post-game comments, "We have to get some guys that understand that it′s not just about points and minutes, and care about all aspects of the game."<ref name=ap20161122/> L. J. Peak led the Hoyas with 18 points<ref name=ap20161122/> and Rodney Pryor finished with 14.<ref name=ap20161122/> For the second straight season, the Hoyas opened with a 2–3 record.

The loss to Wisconsin relegated the Hoyas to the third-place game, in which they faced [[2016–17 Oklahoma State Cowboys basketball team|Oklahoma State]] the next day. Oklahoma State had beaten [[2016–17 UConn Huskies men's basketball team|UConn]] in the quarterfinals, but then suffered a one-sided defeat at the hands of No. 4 [[2016–17 North Carolina Tar Heels men's basketball team|North Carolina]] in the semifinals. The Cowboys began the game with a sluggish and lackluster effort that led Oklahoma State head coach [[Brad Underwood]] to call an early time out, slam down his clipboard, berate his team, and replace four starters with bench players.<ref name=ap20161123>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Oklahoma State - Game Recap - November 23, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400926709|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Underwood's admonishment and the lineup change sparked much greater energy among his players, who presented the Hoyas with a strong pressure defense the rest of the way.<ref name=ap20161123/> This time, turnovers were the decisive factor: The Hoyas fell victim to sloppy ball-handling, and Oklahoma State forced 14 turnovers – 11 of them steals – in the first half alone<ref name=ap20161123/> and led 50–35 at the half.<ref name=ap20161123/> For the game overall, Georgetown shot 51 percent from the field, but Oklahoma State scored 41 points off 28 turnovers,<ref name=ap20161123/> including 19 steals,<ref name=ap20161123/> and had a 59–16 advantage in points off the bench.<ref name=ap20161123/> Rodney Pryor scored 15 points<ref name=ap20161123/> and Bradley Hayes 13,<ref name=ap20161123/> and Akoy Agau scored in double figures for the first time as a Hoya, finishing with 11 points,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Oklahoma State - Box Score - November 23, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400926709|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> but the Cowboys won 97–70.<ref name=ap20161123/> Georgetown finished in fourth place in the tournament and fell to 2–4 on the season. It was Georgetown's worst start since the [[1971–72 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1971–1972 team]] opened 1–5 on its way to a 3–23 final record.

The Hoyas returned to the Verizon Center to sweep a three-game homestand, defeating [[2016–17 Howard Bison basketball team|Howard]], [[2016–17 Coppin State Eagles men's basketball team|Coppin State]], and [[2016–17 Elon Phoenix men's basketball team|Elon]]; the Elon game, by far the closest of the three, was a part of the annual [[BB&T Classic]], in which Georgetown made both its third consecutive appearance and third appearance overall and improved its all-time record in the Classic to 3–0. Rodney Pryor led the Hoyas in all three games; he scored 26 points against Howard<ref name=boxscore20161127>{{Cite web|title=Howard vs. Georgetown - Box Score - November 27, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400919648|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and 30 points against Coppin State, tying his career high with seven three-pointers,<ref name=ap20161130>{{Cite web|title=Coppin State vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - November 30, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919650|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and he finished with 23 points against Elon.<ref name=ap20161204>{{Cite web|title=Elon vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - December 4, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919617|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> L. J. Peak scored 14 points against Howard<ref name=boxscore20161127/> and had a career-high 10 assists<ref name=ap20161130/> against Coppin State – the first Georgetown player to have double-digit assists since [[Markel Starks]] had 11 on [[2013–14 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|March 3, 2014]].<ref name=ap20161130/> Peak followed that performance with a 22-point game against Elon.<ref name=ap20161204/> Akoy Agau scored 14 against Howard,<ref name=boxscore20161127/> a new high for him as a Hoya, and Tre Campbell finished with 12 points in the Howard game.<ref name=boxscore20161127/> Bradley Hayes had 10 points, seven rebounds, five assists, and three blocked shots against Coppin State,<ref name=ap20161130/> while Jessie Govan grabbed a career-best 11 rebounds in the Coppin State game<ref name=ap20161130/> and scored 13 points against Elon.<ref name=ap20161204/> Against Coppin State, the Hoyas shot 45.2 percent from three-point range, making a season-high 14 three-pointers on 31 attempts.<ref name=ap20161130/>

Six days after beating Elon, Georgetown traveled to [[Miami]] to meet [[2016–17 La Salle Explorers men's basketball team|La Salle]] – a team Georgetown had played only twice since [[1964–65 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1965]]<ref name=ap20161210>{{Cite web|title=La Salle vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - December 10, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400918400|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> – in the Hoophall Miami Invitational.<ref name=ap20161210/> The Hoyas broke a tie and ran away from the Explorers with a late run in the final 8:44 to win,<ref name=ap20161210/> improving their all-time record against La Salle to 10–15<ref name=ap20161210/> and extending their winning streak to four, as L. J. Peak scored 24 points<ref name=ap20161210/> Rodney Pryor 19,<ref name=ap20161210/> Jesse Govan 18,<ref name=boxscore20161210>{{Cite web|title=La Salle vs. Georgetown - Box Score - December 10, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400918400|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and Jagan Moseley scored in double figures for the first time as a Hoya with 14 points,<ref name=boxscore20161210/> while Marcus Derrickson contributed nine points and eight rebounds.<ref name=boxscore20161210/>

On December 12, two days after the La Salle game, John Thompson III announced that [[Isaac Copeland]] had decided to transfer to [[Nebraska Cornhuskers men's basketball|Nebraska]] at the end of the semester.<ref name=wang20161212>{{Cite news|title=Georgetown basketball's Isaac Copeland to transfer|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/sports/wp/2016/12/12/georgetown-basketballs-isaac-copeland-to-transfer/|access-date=2022-10-16|issn=0190-8286}}</ref> Copeland gave no reason for leaving Georgetown, but the arrival of Rodney Pryor and increased playing time for reserves Marcus Derrickson and Kaleb Johnson as well as his own declining performance and injuries had led to reduced playing time for him.<ref name=wang20161212/>

After another week off following the La Salle game, the Hoyas journeyed to the [[Carrier Dome]] to face [[2016–17 Syracuse Orange men's basketball team|Syracuse]] – [[Georgetown–Syracuse men's basketball rivalry|their archrival]] throughout the 34-season history of the [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|original Big East Conference]] of 1979–2013 – on a snowy day on which Syracuse honored former Orange great [[Dwayne Washington (basketball)|Dwayne "Pearl" Washington]], who had died of cancer in April 2016.<ref name=kekis20161217>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Syracuse - Game Recap - December 17, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400915316|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Syracuse jumped out to an 11–4 lead, its largest of the game, in the first 5:08,<ref name=kekis20161217/> but Georgetown came back and L. J. Peak sank a basket to tie the game at 31–31 with two minutes left until the intermission,<ref name=kekis20161217/> in part thanks to Peak's 12 first-half points.<ref name=kekis20161217/> The game was tied 33–33 at halftime,<ref name=kekis20161217/> but Georgetown pulled ahead to its largest lead of the game, 67–60, with only 2:36 left to play.<ref name=kekis20161217/> The Orange closed to 69–66 with 1:04 left,<ref name=kekis20161217/> but the Hoyas hit nine free throws in the final 38 seconds to come away with a 78–71 victory,<ref name=kekis20161217/> their sixth over the Orange in the last eight meetings.<ref name=kekis20161217/> Peak had a double-double with 23 points and 11 rebounds<ref name=kekis20161217/> and Rodney Pryor scored 20 points.<ref name=kekis20161217/> Georgetown, which entered the game averaging 28.5 trips to the free-throw line per game and shooting 77.5 percent in free throws,<ref name=kekis20161217/> went 22-of-25 from the free-throw line, while Syracuse made only 14 of its 25 free throw attempts.<ref name=kekis20161217/> The Hoyas improved their all-time record against Syracuse to 43–49,<ref name=kekis20161217/> their all-time road record against Syracuse to 13–30,<ref name=kekis20161217/> and their record against the Orange under John Thompson III to 11–7.<ref name=kekis20161217/>

Georgetown closed out the nonconference portion of its season by returning to the Verizon Center to defeat [[2016–17 UNC Greensboro Spartans men's basketball team|UNC Greensboro]] in a game in which Jesse Govan went 9-for-13 (69.2 percent) from the field, including 2-for-2 in three-pointers, and had 20 points, nine rebounds, five assists, and four blocks,<ref name=ap20161222>{{Cite web|title=UNC Greensboro vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - December 22, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400916897|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> while L. J. Peak contributed 16 points,<ref>{{Cite web|title=UNC Greensboro vs. Georgetown - Box Score - December 22, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400916897|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Marcus Derrickson scored 15 points,<ref name=ap20161222/> and Rodney Pryor added 12.<ref name=ap20161222/> The Hoyas had won five straight to enter the Big East season with a record of 8–4.

===Conference schedule===

The Hoyas opened the Big East season with a loss at [[2016–17 Marquette Golden Eagles men's basketball team|Marquette]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Marquette - Game Recap - December 28, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919659|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> in which Rodney Pryor finished with 23 points,<ref name=boxscore20161228>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. St. John's - Box Score - January 13, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400840262|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Jesse Govan scored 11,<ref name=boxscore20161228/> and Marcus Derrickson came off the bench for 11.<ref name=boxscore20161228/> They then came home to host their third ranked opponent of the year, No. 17 [[2016–17 Xavier Musketeers men's basketball team|Xavier]], at the Verizon Center on [[New Year's Eve]] 2016. Xavier was one of four Big East teams ranked in the Top 17 at the time.<ref name=ap20170101>{{Cite web|title=Xavier vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - December 31, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919661|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Peak scored 16 points in the first half, and the underdog Hoyas led 38–36 at halftime<ref name=ap20170101/> and pulled out to a six-point lead early in the second half.<ref name=ap20170101/> Xavier came back to tie the game at 54–54, but Peak completed a three-point play – scoring his last points of the game – to put Georgetown ahead 57–54 with 11:41 left to play.<ref name=ap20170101/> Xavier increasingly used a 1-3-1 [[zone defense]] as the second half progressed, and this gave the Musketeers greater defensive success against the Hoyas.<ref name=ap20170101/> Xavier took the lead for good at 62–59 with 8:23 remaining during a 13-5 scoring run that gave the Musketeers their largest lead of the game, 74–62, with 3:58 left to play.<ref name=ap20170101/> Rodney Pryor led a Georgetown comeback by scoring 10 points in a row, but his potential game-tying three-pointer missed with Xavier leading 77–74 and 24 seconds remaining. Although Georgetown held Xavier to 39 percent shooting from the field,<ref name=ap20170101/> and rendered Xavier's leading scorer, junior guard [[Trevon Bluiett]], ineffective throughout the game,<ref name=ap20170101/> Musketeer redshirt sophomore guard [[Edmond Sumner]], playing on his birthday, scored a career-high 28 points.<ref name=ap20170101/> From the free-throw line, Xavier went 29-for-38 (76.3 percent)<ref name=ap20170101/> with Sumner alone going 14-for-17 (82.4 percent),<ref name=ap20170101/> while Georgetown as a team shot 14-for-23 (60.9 percent) from the line.<ref name=ap20170101/> Georgetown shot 50 percent from the field, and Peak finished with a team-high 21 points,<ref name=ap20170101/> Pryor with 20,<ref name=ap20170101/> and Derrickson with 12,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Xavier vs. Georgetown - Box Score - December 31, 2016 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400919661|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> but Xavier held on to win, 81–76.<ref name=ap20170101/> Georgetown had its first 0–2 start in Big East play since [[2012–13 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|the 2012–2013 season]].<ref name=ap20170101/>

A visit to [[2016–17 Providence Friars men's basketball team|Providence]] four days later to play the first game of 2017 resulted in a third loss<ref name=ap20170104>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Providence - Game Recap - January 4, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919667|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and Georgetown's first 0–3 start in conference play since [[1999–2000 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|the 1999–2000 season]]. Marcus Derrickson had a career-high 26 points,<ref name=ap20170104/> Rodney Pryor scored 16,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Providence - Box Score - January 4, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400919667|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and Akoy Agau had his first career double-double with 12 points and a career-best 12 rebounds,<ref name=ap20170104/> but Georgetown remained winless on the road against the Friars since [[2011–12 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|February 18, 2012]].<ref name=ap20170101/> The Hoyas then hosted their second ranked conference opponent of the season, No. 18 [[2016–17 Butler Bulldogs men's basketball team|Butler]], which three days earlier had upset No. 1 [[2016–17 Villanova Wildcats men's basketball team|Villanova]].<ref name=ap20170107>{{Cite web|title=Butler vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - January 7, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919669|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Georgetown led 32–31 at halftime.<ref name=ap20170107/> With a minute left to play, the Hoyas held a 66–63 lead,<ref name=ap20170107/><ref name=playbyplay20170107>{{Cite web|title=Butler vs. Georgetown - Play-By-Play - January 7, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/playbyplay/_/gameId/400919669|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> but Butler sophomore center Nate Fowler's three-pointer tied the game at 66–66 with 58 seconds to play.<ref name=ap20170107/><ref name=playbyplay20170107/> Jagan Moseley hit two free throws with 38 seconds on the clock to give the Hoyas a 68–66 lead,<ref name=playbyplay20170107/> but Fowler's two free throws with eight seconds left again tied the game at 68–68.<ref name=ap20170107/><ref name=playbyplay20170107/> Georgetown had a chance to avoid overtime and pull off an upset, but L. J. Peak's attempt at a buzzer-beating turnaround jumper as time expired in regulation bounced off the rim.<ref name=ap20170107/> Butler never trailed in overtime and took the lead for good with 3:04 to play on two free throws by redshirt senior guard [[Kethan Savage]].<ref name=ap20170107/> The Bulldogs won, 85–76, their third consecutive victory over the Hoyas.<ref name=ap20170107/> The Hoyas outscored the Bulldogs 40–20 in the paint<ref name=ap20170107/> and Butler shot only 39.1 percent from the field,<ref name=ap20170107/> but the Bulldogs stayed in the game on 10-of-20 shooting from three-point range.<ref name=ap20170107/> Peak scored a team-high 21 points,<ref name=ap20170107/> Jagan Moseley contributed a career-best 20,<ref name=ap20170107/> Marcus Derrickson contributed 14 points,<ref name=boxscore20170107>{{Cite web|title=Butler vs. Georgetown - Box Score - January 7, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400919669|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and Bradley Hayes narrowly missed a double-double with 10 points and nine rebounds,<ref name=boxscore20170107/> but Rodney Pryor, the Big East's scoring co-leader entering the game, averaging 19.8 points, went scoreless on 0-for-8 shooting against a spirited defensive effort by Butler freshman guard [[Kamar Baldwin]], who also scored a career-high 16 points for the Bulldogs.<ref name=ap20170107/> Georgetown saw its record fall to 8–8 and opened its conference season 0–4 for the first time since [[1998–99 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|the 1998–1999 season]],<ref name=ap20170107/> and, along with [[2016–17 DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball team|DePaul]], was one of two teams still winless in the Big East.<ref name=ap20170107/>

Two days after the loss to Butler, Georgetown's four-game homestand continued with its first conference win, a runaway victory over [[2016–17 St. John's Red Storm men's basketball team|St. John's]] – the Hoyas′ twelfth straight home win over the Red Storm – with L. J. Peak scoring 16 points that included a 10-for-10 free-throw shooting performance,<ref name=ap20170109>{{Cite web|title=St. John's vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - January 9, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919674|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Rodney Pryor and Jagan Moseley each scoring 13 points,<ref name=ap20170109/> and Marcus Derrickson adding 11.<ref name=ap20170109/> A break from conference action followed, as [[2016–17 UConn Huskies men's basketball team|UConn]] visited the Verizon Center to conclude a home-and-home series begun [[2015–16 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|the previous season]]. The Hoyas and Huskies were charter members of the [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|original Big East Conference]] in [[1979–80 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1979]] and had met each season throughout that conference's 34-year history, but the rivalry had lapsed when Georgetown left the conference in the summer of 2013 to join the new [[Big East Conference]] while UConn remained behind in the old conference, renamed the [[American Athletic Conference]] and marketed as "the American;" the two-season home-and-home series revived play between the teams after a two-season absence. UConn had won the previous year, but this time the Hoyas overcame a 14-point second-half deficit to beat the Huskies and improve their all-time record against UConn to 36–30.<ref name=ap20170114>{{Cite web|title=UConn vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - January 14, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400916584|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> L. J. Peak scored 21 points, 16 of them in the second half,<ref name=ap20170114/> Jesse Govan came off the bench to finish with 15,<ref name=ap20170114/> and Rodney Pryor had 14.<ref name=ap20170114/> Georgetown's two-game winning streak and four-game homestand both came to an end two days later, when Providence visited Georgetown and won easily to sweep the regular-season series between the teams and stretch its winning streak against the Hoyas to six.<ref name=ap20170116>{{Cite web|title=Providence vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - January 16, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919688|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Peak scored 13 points<ref name=ap20170116/> and Pryor 12,<ref name=ap20170116/> but the Hoyas as a team shot only 18-for-55 (32.7 percent) from the field and only 5-for-23 (21.7 percent) from three-point range against the Friars.<ref name=ap20170116/>

With a conference record of 1–5 and an overall record of 10–9, Georgetown began a stretch of three straight games in seven days against ranked conference opponents. First they visited No. 22 Xavier. The Musketeers entered the game having lost three games in a row, all against ranked Big East teams, their longest losing streak in three years.<ref name=ap20170122>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Xavier - Game Recap - January 22, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919693|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Xavier clung to a 34–33 lead at halftime, but pulled out to a 12-point advantage in the second half.<ref name=ap20170122/> The Hoyas came back to tie the game at 58–58, but Xavier then went on a decisive 12–3 scoring run to  take a 70–61 lead.<ref name=ap20170122/> Rodney Pryor scored 23 points<ref name=ap20170122/> and L. J. Peak finished with 12, but fouling and rebounding undid the Hoyas;<ref name=ap20170122/> the Musketeers repeatedly drew fouls by driving the basket and went 36-for-49 from the free-throw line, while the Hoyas made 11 out of 14 free throws.<ref name=ap20170122/> Xavier won 86–75,<ref name=ap20170122/> handing Georgetown its sixth loss in seven games<ref name=ap20170122/> and dropping the Hoyas to 10–10 on the season and 1–6 in the Big East.<ref name=ap20170122/> In play against ranked teams, Georgetown had lost four straight games and nine of its last ten.<ref name=ap20170125>{{Cite web|title=Creighton vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - January 25, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919696|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref>

Georgetown next returned to the Verizon Center to host No. 16 [[2016–17 Creighton Bluejays men's basketball team|Creighton]]. The Bluejays were the second-best shooting team in [[NCAA Division I]] at 52.8 percent from the field,<ref name=ap20170125/> and tenth in three-point shooting at 40.8 percent,<ref name=ap20170125/> but had suffered a major loss when a season-ending knee injury sidelined their [[point guard]], senior Maurice Watson Jr., nine days earlier during a game against Xavier.<ref name=ap20170125/> Jonathan Mulmore made his first start as a Hoya.<ref name=ap20170125/> Rodney Pryor had an outstanding first half in which he dunked several times, sank two of his three three-pointers, and scored 15 points.<ref name=ap20170125/> Thanks in part to a 13–2 scoring run,<ref name=ap20170125/> Georgetown led 39–27 at the half.<ref name=ap20170125/> The Hoyas extended their lead to as many as 22 points in the second half<ref name=ap20170125/> and never led by fewer than 14 points during the last 15:32 of the game.<ref name=ap20170125/> Georgetown cruised to a 71–51 upset victory.<ref name=ap20170125/> Creighton shot only 34.5 percent from the field and only 1-for-18 (5.6 percent) from three-point range,<ref name=ap20170125/> and it was the Bluejays′ lowest-scoring game of the season.<ref name=ap20170125/> Georgetown outrebounded Creighton 47–36.<ref name=ap20170125/> L. J. Peak scored 20 points,<ref name=ap20170125/> Pryor finished with 18,<ref name=boxscore20170125>{{Cite web|title=Creighton vs. Georgetown - Box Score - January 25, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400919696|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> and Jesse Govan added 15.<ref name=boxscore20170125/> The win was Georgetown's first conference victory over any team other than [[DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball|DePaul]] and St. John's – perennially the two teams at the bottom of the conference's standings – since a win over [[2015–16 Creighton Bluejays men's basketball team|Creighton]] on [[2015–16 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|January 26, 2016]],<ref name=ap20170125/> and it improved Georgetown's conference record to 2–6, allowing the Hoyas to avoid their first 1–7 conference start since the 1998–1999 season.<ref name=ap20170125/>

The Hoyas traveled to [[Indianapolis]] to face No. 11 Butler in their next game. Butler – winner of four straight games overall and 14 straight at home, including 11–0 thus far in the 2016–2017 season<ref name=ap20170128>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Butler - Game Recap - January 28, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919700|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> – led 41–40 at halftime.<ref name=ap20170128/> During one stretch in the second half, Rodney Pryor, despite playing with four fouls, scored 11 straight points, nine of them on three straight contested three-pointers, giving Georgetown a 72–65 lead.<ref name=ap20170128/> The Bulldogs then closed the gap, scoring seven straight points to tie the game at 72–72.<ref name=ap20170128/> The Hoyas led 79–77 with 1:03 to play when Jesse Govan hit a long, unexpected three-pointer – only the third three-pointer he had ever made in Big East play – to give Georgetown an 82–77 lead.<ref name=ap20170128/> The Bulldogs never had another chance to tie or take the lead, and Georgetown won 85–81.<ref name=ap20170128/> During the three-year tenure of Butler head coach [[Chris Holtmann]], the Bulldogs had won all 30 previous games in which they had scored 80 or more points.<ref name=ap20170128/> The Hoyas shot 63.8 percent from the field for the game and 72.7 percent in the second half.<ref name=ap20170128/> L. J. Peak scored 22 points<ref name=ap20170128/> and Pryor 20,<ref name=ap20170128/> while Govan went 8-for-9 from the field overall and 3-for-3 in three-pointers and tied his season high by finishing with 20 points.<ref name=ap20170128/>

The back-to-back wins over Creighton and Butler gave the Hoyas a 3–3 record against ranked teams for the season<ref name=ap20170128/> and, with a weaker part of their schedule coming up, raised hopes that the team could turn its season around after a difficult start over the first three months.<ref name=ap20170128/> The Hoyas concluded January by winning their third game in a row, defeating [[2016–17 DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball team|DePaul]] in a close one at the Verizon Center thanks largely to L. J. Peak scoring five points in the final minute and Jesse Govan blocking a shot with 40 seconds to play.<ref name=ap20170131>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. DePaul - Game Recap - January 31, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919703|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Rodney Pryor scored a game-high 26 points,<ref name=ap20170131/> Govan finished with 14,<ref name=ap20170131/> and Peak contributed 13.<ref name=ap20170131/> The victory was Georgetown's 20th over DePaul in the last 21 meetings between the teams and improved Georgetown's record to 13–10 overall, 4–6 in the Big East, but the Hoyas were destined to win only one more game all season.

Peak scored 18 points, Rodney Pryor had 13, and Marcus Derrickson finished with nine points and eight rebounds.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Seton Hall vs. Georgetown - Game Recap - February 4, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919707|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> On February 6, as the Hoyas headed north through [[Howard County, Maryland|Howard County]], [[Maryland]], on [[Interstate 95]] on their way to [[Pennsylvania]] to play No. 2 [[2016–17 Villanova Wildcats men's basketball team|Villanova]], their team bus struck the rear of a [[sport-utility vehicle]], causing the SUV to veer off the highway and overturn.<ref name=allen20170207>{{Cite news|title=Georgetown basketball team's bus crashed while traveling to Villanova|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/dc-sports-bog/wp/2017/02/07/georgetown-basketball-teams-bus-crashed-while-traveling-to-villanova/|access-date=2022-10-16|issn=0190-8286}}</ref> The team and its staff got off the bus to assist the two occupants of the SUV, who were taken to a hospital, then boarded another bus to finish their journey.<ref name=allen20170207/> No one aboard the bus requested medical attention,<ref name=allen20170207/> but when the Hoyas met Villanova at [[Finneran Pavilion|The Pavilion]] the following afternoon, Tre Campbell sat out with a banged knee and John Thompson III  was observed hobbling along the sideline in apparent pain.<ref name=ap20170208>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. Villanova - Game Recap - February 7, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400919711|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> The Wildcats missed six of their first seven three-point attempts,<ref name=ap20170208/> but then Villanova senior guard [[Josh Hart (basketball)|Josh Hart]] sparked an offensive surge by hitting three three-pointers and scoring 17 first-half points;<ref name=ap20170208/> Villanova took a 17-point first-half lead<ref name=ap20170208/> and still led 43–28 at halftime.<ref name=ap20170208/> In the second half, Hart fell silent on offense and the Hoyas made a comeback bid, mounting a 17–4 scoring run that cut a Wildcat 17-point lead to 60–58 with 3:49 left to play.<ref name=ap20170208/> With Georgetown threatening an upset, Hart regained his form on offense, hitting two clutch shots, a three-pointer and a layup, to give the Wildcats a 70–61 lead.<ref name=ap20170208/> Hart finished with a game-high 25 points and Villanova won 75–64<ref name=ap20170208/> for its 48th straight victory at The Pavilion.<ref name=ap20170208/> Peak scored 21 points<ref name=ap20170208/> and Pryor had 20 points and nine rebounds,<ref name=ap20170208/> but the back-to-back losses dropped Georgetown to 13–12 overall and 4–8 in the Big East.

J. In reporting the results of the final game against Villanova, the [[Associated Press]] referred to "the disaster of Thompson′s 13th season on the Hilltop [i.e., at Georgetown],"<ref name=ap20170304/> and when a reporter tried to ask John Thompson III questions about the future of the Georgetown men's basketball program as it faced a likely second consecutive losing season, a team spokesman interrupted, saying "Leave it to game-related questions, please."<ref name=ap20170304/>

===Big East tournament===
{{main|2017 Big East men's basketball tournament}}

With a No. 9 seed in the [[2017 Big East men's basketball tournament|2017 Big East tournament]] at Madison Square Garden, Georgetown faced eighth-seeded St. John's in the first round. Both schools were charter members of the original Big East Conference when it was created in [[1979–80 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1979]], and it was their seventh meeting in the tournament since it began in [[1980 Big East men's basketball tournament|1980]].<ref name=ap20170308>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. St. John's - Game Recap - March 8, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/400945520|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> Former Georgetown head coach [[John Thompson (basketball)|John Thompson Jr.]], and former Georgetown great [[Allen Iverson]], both members of the [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame]], attended the game.<ref name=ap20170308/> In the original Big East's heyday in the mid-1980s, when St. John's head coach [[Chris Mullin (basketball)|Chris Mullin]] had played for the Red Storm and John Thompson III's father, John Thompson Jr., had coached the Hoyas, the two schools had been national powers and great rivals, and both teams entered the game aware of this history.<ref name=ap20170308/> St. John's made only five of its first 21 shots from the field,<ref name=ap20170308/> but led 38–34 at halftime,<ref name=ap20170308/> and also led for most of the second half.<ref name=ap20170308/> With 8:35 left to play and St. John's ahead 59–55, the game briefly took on the character of the very physical games of the original Big East in the 1980s when Red Storm junior forward Amar Alibegović fouled L. J. Peak hard under the basket and a shoving match ensued between several players, resulting in the officials calling a [[flagrant foul]] against Alibegović and [[technical foul]]s against both Chris Mullin and Georgetown assistant coach [[Patrick Ewing Jr.]], a former Georgetown player whose father, [[Patrick Ewing]], had played against Mullin as Georgetown's center at the peak of the 1980s rivalry between the teams.<ref name=ap20170308/> After the scuffle, Peak made one free throw to cut the Red Storm's lead to 59–56.<ref name=ap20170308/> After that, the Hoyas got within one point of St. John's three times but could never take the lead.<ref name=ap20170308/> The Red Storm led 74–68 with three minutes to play, but did not score again.<ref name=ap20170308/> In Georgetown's final possession, which began with 6.6 seconds remaining and St. John's clinging to a 74–73 lead,<ref name=ap20170308/> both Peak and Marcus Derrickson missed close-in shots, allowing St. John's to hang on for a 74–73 win.<ref name=ap20170308/> Georgetown's season came to an end, while St. John's snapped a six-year losing streak in the Big East tournament<ref name=ap20170308/> and moved on to face Villanova in the quarterfinals the following day.<ref name=ap20170308/> The Red Storm finished shooting 37.7 percent from the field overall,<ref name=ap20170308/> including 5-for-20 (25 percent) from three-point range,<ref name=ap20170308/> while the Hoyas shot 45.8 percent from the field overall<ref name=ap20170308/> and made five of their 21 three-point shots (23.8 percent).<ref name=ap20170308/> Playing in their last game for Georgetown, Peak scored a game-high 24 points,<ref name=ap20170308/> 22 of them in the second half,<ref name=ap20170308/> and Rodney Pryor contributed 17.<ref name=ap20170308/> Derrickson scored 11 points.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Georgetown vs. St. John's - Box Score - March 8, 2017 - ESPN|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore/_/gameId/400945520|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref>

With a record of 14–18 and having lost their last six games and eight of their last nine, Georgetown received no invitation to either the [[2017 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|NCAA tournament]] or the [[2017 National Invitation Tournament|National Invitation Tournament]] for the second straight year. It was the first time Georgetown had two consecutive losing seasons since [[1971–72 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1971–1972]] and [[1972–73 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1972–1973]], and the first time the Hoyas had received an invitation to neither the NCAA Tournament or the NIT in two consecutive seasons since [[1972–73 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1973]] and [[1973–74 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1974]]. For the second straight season, the Hoyas never made the Top 25 in either the [[Associated Press Poll]] or the [[Coaches Poll]] – the first time that had happened in consecutive seasons since [[2002–03 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2002-2003]] and [[2003–04 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2003-2004]].

===John Thompson III fired===

The failure of the 2016–2017 team, coming on the heels of a similar failure the previous season, left the Georgetown basketball program in turmoil. In his 13 years at Georgetown, John Thompson III had an overall record of 278–151, with 11 winning seasons,<ref name=santamariahoffman20170324>{{Cite web|date=2017-03-24|title=John Thompson III Fired After 2 Consecutive Losing Seasons|url=https://thehoya.com/john-thompson-iii-fired-after-two-consecutive-losing-seasons/|access-date=2022-10-16|language=en-US}}</ref> eight appearances in the NCAA Tournament and three in the NIT. Since the notorious loss<ref name=steinberg20170309>{{Cite web|last=Steinberg|first=Russell|date=2017-03-09|title=Georgetown's past, present, and future is at stake with John Thompson III decision|url=https://www.sbnation.com/college-basketball/2017/3/9/14866240/georgetown-hoyas-coaching-decision-john-thompson-iii-big-east-tournament|access-date=2022-10-16|website=SBNation.com|language=en}}</ref> to 15th-seeded [[2012–13 Florida Gulf Coast Eagles men's basketball team|Florida Gulf Coast]] in the [[2013 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2013 NCAA tournament]], however, Georgetown had endured the worst four-year stretch of his tenure as head coach.<ref name=santamariahoffman20170324/> Those four years coincided with the first four seasons of the new Big East Conference; it consisted of a group of schools brought in from [[mid-major]] conferences combined with some of the less-competitive teams from the original Big East, and the Hoyas and their fans had expected the team to dominate the new conference as its flagship program.<ref name=balthazard20170224/> Instead, over those four years the Hoyas had posted an overall record of 69–62,<ref name=preston20170324>{{Cite web|date=2017-03-24|title=Thompson's firing marks end of era at Georgetown|url=https://wtop.com/sports-columns/2017/03/thompsons-firing-marks-end-era-georgetown/|access-date=2022-10-16|website=WTOP News|language=en}}</ref> and their 32–40 Big East record was third-worst in the conference;<ref name=santamariahoffman20170324/> the Hoyas had no regular-season or conference-tournament championships in the new Big East,<ref name=balthazard20170224/> had missed the NCAA Tournament in three of the new conference's four seasons, had lost in the second game of their lone NCAA appearance – as well as in the second game of their only NIT appearance – and had finished with two consecutive losing seasons in which they had no postseason play whatsoever.<ref name=santamariahoffman20170324/> For the second year in a row, the team had an up-and-down early season and collapsed in February; the 2016–2017 season ended with six consecutive losses, including to DePaul and St. John's – both long the cellar-dwellers of the Big East – and the team's 14–18 record was the worst for Georgetown since the [[1971–72 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1971-1972 team]]'s dismal 3–23 finish.<ref name=santamariahoffman20170324/> Although Thompson emphasized defense, the Hoyas′ defense had been mediocre over its four years in the new Big East, never ranking higher than 110th among the 351 [[NCAA Division I]] teams in defensive efficiency,<ref name=balthazard20170224/> and the 2016–2017 squad's defense statistics were poor: 116th in the defensive efficiency<ref name=balthazard20170224/> and 302nd in fouls committed,<ref name=balthazard20170224/> while allowing opponents 10 offensive rebounds per game.<ref name=balthazard20170224/> On offense, the Hoyas had gone five seasons without ever ranking in the top 50 teams in offensive efficiency,<ref name=balthazard20170224/> and in three seasons had ranked worse than 100th.<ref name=balthazard20170224/>

By late February, signs began to appear in the student section at the Verizon Center and on the road at Madison Square Garden reading "Fire Thompson" and "Degioia Do Your Job" – a plea for Georgetown University President [[John J. DeGioia]] to fire Thompson – and cheers of "Fire Thompson!" became common from the stands.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Hadar|first=Roey|date=2017-03-05|title=View from the Student Section: "I'll kick your f*cking ass"|url=https://www.casualhoya.com/2017/3/5/14817856/georgetown-hoyas-student-tyler-crawford-villanova-wildcats|access-date=2022-10-16|website=Casual Hoya|language=en}}</ref><ref name=balthazard20170224>{{Cite web|date=2017-02-24|title=COMMENTARY: Students Lose Faith in Basketball Team|url=https://thehoya.com/commentary-students-lose-faith-in-basketball-team/|access-date=2022-10-16|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=thehoya20170317>{{Cite web|date=2017-03-17|title=EDITORIAL: Georgetown Basketball Must Confront Off-Court Issues|url=https://thehoya.com/editorial-georgetown-basketball-must-confront-off-campus-issues/|access-date=2022-10-16|language=en-US}}</ref> In early March, Georgetown students launched a petition demanding that the university fire Thompson;<ref name=santamariahoffman20170324/> it garnered 1,700 signatures by mid-March.<ref name=thehoya20170317/> Adding fuel to the fire, Thompson's attempt to address Georgetown's lack of a true [[point guard]] since the graduation of [[Markel Starks]] in 2014 by recruiting [[Tremont Waters]], an elite point guard prospect, for the following season failed when Waters requested his release from Georgetown on March 11,<ref>{{Cite web|date=2017-03-12|title=Georgetown commit T. Waters wants release|url=https://www.espn.com/recruiting/basketball/story/_/id/18886342/four-star-point-guard-tremont-waters-requests-release-georgetown|access-date=2022-10-16|website=ESPN.com|language=en}}</ref> highlighting to the fan base how much of its star power the Georgetown program had lost since its 2007 Final Four appearance.<ref name=thehoya20170317/> More negative publicity arose when school financial disclosures revealed that Thompson had received annual pay increases from 2008 to through 2014, resulting in a salary of $3.6 million a year that likely made him one of the ten most highly compensated college basketball coaches in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Hadar|first=Roey|date=2017-03-20|title=John Thompson III's salary is higher than we thought|url=https://www.casualhoya.com/2017/3/20/14976582/john-thompson-iii-salary-is-higher-than-thought-georgetown-hoyas-basketball-coach|access-date=2022-10-16|website=Casual Hoya|language=en}}</ref> Amid a rising chorus of criticism by Georgetown students and alumni of Thompson's performance, and press articles by students and [[ESPN]] describing dissatisfaction among Georgetown students and alumni with the direction of the men's basketball program,<ref name=santamariahoffman20170324/> Georgetown University announced on March 23 that it had fired Thompson, bringing his 13-year tenure as head coach to an end.<ref name=tracy20170323>{{Cite news|last=Tracy|first=Marc|date=2017-03-23|title=John Thompson III Is Out as Georgetown Coach|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/03/23/sports/ncaabasketball/georgetown-john-thompson-coach-fired.html|access-date=2022-10-16|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

name=casualhoya20170322/> – had no such straightforward explanation.<ref name=steinberg20170309/>

While the team that centered around the 2011 recruiting class's Greg Whittington and [[Otto Porter Jr.]] showed signs of potential greatness,<ref name=casualhoya20161212>{{Cite web|last=overthehilltop|date=2016-12-12|title=Isaac Copeland's Transfer and the Arc of Georgetown Basketball|url=https://www.casualhoya.com/2016/12/12/13932670/isaac-copeland-transfer-georgetown-hoyas|access-date=2022-10-16|website=Casual Hoya|language=en}}</ref> it never reached the heights of the 2006–2007 Final Four team, and after Porter departed for the NBA in 2013 after his sophomore season, Thompson's recruiting efforts paid fewer and fewer dividends.<ref name=casualhoya20161212/> Thompson remained committed to his "[[Princeton offense]]" despite its growing obsolescence in the face of the evolution of the college game,<ref name=niessen20170323/> and his adherence to it harmed his recruiting efforts, as potential recruits sought opportunities elsewhere under systems that better fit their playing style and showcased the athletic abilities that NBA scouts favored.<ref name=thamel20170403>{{Cite web|last=Thamel|first=Pete |author-link=Pete Thamel |title=Georgetown is taking a big gamble in hiring Patrick Ewing |url=https://www.si.com/college/2017/04/04/georgetown-patrick-ewing-thompson |access-date=2022-10-16|website=[[Sports Illustrated]] |language=en-us}}</ref> Washington, D.C., and its suburbs remained a hotbed of high-school basketball talent, but Thompson had markedly less success in recruiting Washington-area players than his predecessors John Thompson Jr. and Craig Esherick; observers noted that Villanova had built the dominant team and perennial winner in the new Big East Conference – a team that made deep runs annually in the NCAA Tournament and won the national championship in [[2010 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2016]] – at least partially by recruiting two star players from Washington's Maryland suburbs, guards [[Josh Hart (basketball)|Josh Hart]] from [[Silver Spring, Maryland|Silver Spring]]<ref name=ap20170304/> and [[Kris Jenkins (basketball)|Kris Jenkins]] from [[Upper Marlboro, Maryland|Upper Marlboro]];<ref name=ap20170304/> both had grown up as Hoya fans, but Thompson lost out to Villanova head coach [[Jay Wright (basketball)|Jay Wright]] in recruiting Hart and never pursued Jenkins.<ref name=balthazard20170224/> Under Thompson, the program had a high number of players transfer to other schools,<ref name=thamel20170402>{{Cite web|last=Thamel|first=Pete |author-link=Pete Thamel |title=Georgetown seemingly has no plan in coaching search |url=https://www.si.com/college/2017/04/02/georgetown-coaching-search-hoyas-thompson|access-date=2022-10-16|website=[[Sports Illustrated]]|language=en-us}}</ref> finding that under Thompson they had too little playing time and few opportunities to showcase their athleticism.

The dismissal of both Greg Whittington and [[Joshua Smith (basketball)|Joshua Smith]] from the [[2013–14 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2013–14 team]] could explain that team's failure, but Thompson's declining success in recruiting players who fit into his system and who would develop successfully at the college level began to affect the program's success.<ref name=balthazard20170224/> The highly touted 2014 recruiting class – which included Tre Campbell, Trey Mourning, L. J. Peak, and Paul White – despite some success in [[2014–15 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|its first season]], also was notable for is lack of development on the court.<ref name=casualhoya20161212/> Only Peak showed progress as a junior,<ref name=casualhoya20161212/> and only Mourning remained at Georgetown for a full four years of collegiate eligibility. The glory years of Georgetown's men's basketball program had become too distant to resonate with potential recruits,<ref name=balthazard20170224/> and without NBA-caliber talent after Porter's departure,<ref name=casualhoya20161212/> the once-proud Georgetown program had gone from a perennial national power to consistently mediocre performances that culminated in two straight losing seasons and declining fan interest and attendance at home games;<ref name=preston20170324/><ref name=thamel20170402/><ref name=niessen20170323/> for two straight years, Georgetown had struggled to fill even half the seats for its home games at the Verizon Center.<ref name=thehoya20170317/>

===Patrick Ewing hired===

Rather than fire Thompson soon after the Hoyas′ season ended, Georgetown waited until two weeks later to announce his termination, by which time some top options for the head coaching position already had accepted offers elsewhere.<ref name=thamel20170402/>  Georgetown athletic director Lee Reed and [[Paul Tagliabue]], a former Georgetown player and one-time commissioner of the [[National Football League]], led the effort to find a new head coach,<ref name=thamel20170402/> but observers came to the conclusion that the university had no plan in place for who it wanted to succeed Thompson before it fired him, making the school's search for a successor appear bumbling.<ref name=thamel20170402/>  [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish men's basketball|Notre Dame's]] [[Mike Brey]], [[Xavier Musketeers men's basketball|Xavier's]] [[Chris Mack (basketball)|Chris Mack]], and [[Texas Longhorns men's basketball|Texas's]] [[Shaka Smart]] all rebuffed Georgetown's inquiries,<ref name=thamel20170402/> and [[Harvard Crimson men's basketball|Harvard]]′s [[Tommy Amaker]] privately expressed disinterest in the job because of his concerns over internal politics at Georgetown, fearing that the influence that John Thompson III's father, John Thompson Jr., still wielded over the program despite having resigned as head coach in [[1998–99 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|January 1999]] could lead to a negative political environment for any new head coach.<ref name=thamel20170402/> Georgetown informed recently fired [[Indiana Hoosiers men's basketball|Indiana]] head coach [[Tom Crean (basketball)|Tom Crean]] that he was not a candidate,<ref name=thamel20170402/> but the names of [[Providence Friars men's basketball|Providence's]] [[Ed Cooley]] – who made clear that he had no desire to leave Providence<ref name=thamel20170402/> – [[Rhode Island Rams men's basketball|Rhode Island's]] [[Danny Hurley]], [[Minnesota Golden Gophers men's basketball|Minnesota's]] [[Richard Pitino]], [[Duke Blue Devils men's basketball|Duke]] assistant coach [[Jeff Capel]], [[USC Trojans men's basketball|USC's]] [[Andy Enfield]], [[South Carolina Gamecocks men's basketball|South Carolina's]] [[Frank Martin (basketball)|Frank Martin]], and [[Charlotte Hornets]] assistant coach and Georgetown alumnus [[Patrick Ewing]] all were mentioned in the swirl of media speculation that followed Thompson's firing.<ref name=thamel20170402/>

On April 3, 2017, Georgetown announced that it had hired Patrick Ewing as its next head basketball coach.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Smith|first=Erick|title=Patrick Ewing hired as coach of Georgetown|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/ncaab/bigeast/2017/04/03/patrick-ewing-georgetown-coach/99988542/|access-date=2022-10-16|website=USA TODAY|language=en-US}}</ref> Generally regarded as the greatest player in Georgetown history, Ewing had been Georgetown's star center from [[1981–82 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1981]] to [[1984–85 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1985]], leading the Hoyas to three appearances in the NCAA Tournament championship game and the [[1984 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1984]] national championship, then going on to a [[Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame]] NBA career as a player from 1985 to 2002 and as an assistant coach from 2002 to 2017. It was Ewing's first head coaching job at any level of basketball, and it marked his first foray into college basketball since his graduation from Georgetown in 1985.

===Wrap-up===

Rodney Pryor completed his only season as a Hoya as the team's leading scorer for the year; he started all 32 games, shooting 48.0 percent from the field overall and 41.2 percent in three-pointers, averaging a team-high 18.0 points and leading the team with 5.0 rebounds per game. L. J. Peak also started all 32 games, and he averaged 16.3 points and 3.8 rebounds per game, shooting 48.1 percent from the field overall and 32.7 percent from three-point range. Jesse Govan played in every game, starting 21 of them, shooting 53.0 percent in field-goal attempts and 40.0 percent from three-point range, and he averaged 10.1 points and 5.0 rebounds per game. Marcus Derrickson played in 28 games and started 17 of them, averaging 8.3 points per game on 43.2 percent field-goal shooting overall and 34.4 percent from three-point range, and he had 4.4 rebounds per game. In his only season in action with the Hoyas, Akoy Agau appeared in all 32 games and started eight of them; he ended the season with a field-goal percentage of 50.6 and with per-game averages of 4.5 points and 4.3 rebounds. Bradley Hayes appeared in 25 games, starting 11 of them, and he finished with 4.2 points and 4.0 rebounds per game, shooting 53.4 percent from the field. Jagan Moseley started 20 of the 31 games he played in, and he averaged 4.2 points per game on 45.0 percent shooting from the field – 24.3 percent from beyond the arc – and grabbed 2.2 rebounds per game. Playing in all 32 games, Jonathan Mulmore had 12 starts and averaged 3.6 points and 1.4 rebounds per game, shooting 35.7 percent overall and 34.5 percent in three-pointers. Tre Campbell averaged 3.5 points and 1.2 rebounds in the 20 games he played in, all off the bench, and shot 38.7 percent from the field overall and 34.3 percent from three-point range, while Kaleb Johnson started twice in his 30 appearances, shooting 44.2 percent from the field overall and 25.0 percent in three-pointers, averaging 2.3 points per game and pulling down an average of 1.3 rebounds per game. Reggie Cameron played in 17 games, all off the bench, averaging 1.7 points and 0.9 rebound, and Trey Mourning played in only 10 games, all as a reserve, averaging 0.8 point per game. Before his mid-season transfer, Isaac Copeland played in seven games, started five, and averaged 5.5 points and 3.3 rebounds per game, shooting 27.5 percent from the field. Walk-ons Ra'Mond Hines and George Muresan each played in five games.<ref>[https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/georgetown/2017.html sports-reference.com 2016–17 Georgetown Hoyas Roster and Stats]</ref>

Rodney Pryor, Bradley Hayes, and Reggie Cameron all graduated in 2017. In addition to his lone year at Georgetown, Pryor played for [[Robert Morris Colonials men's basketball|Robert Morris]] in [[2014–15 Robert Morris Colonials men's basketball team|2014–2015]] and [[2015–16 Robert Morris Colonials men's basketball team|2015–2016]], and in his three-season college career he appeared in 96 games, starting 84, shooting 46.5 percent overall from the field and 38.1 percent from three-point range and averaging 17.1 points and 5.8 rebounds per game.<ref>[https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/players/rodney-pryor-1.html sports-reference.com Rodney Pryor College stats Retrieved July 20, 2018]</ref> Hayes played parts of five seasons for Georgetown; an afterthought for the first three, he had his breakout game against [[2014–15 Eastern Washington Eagles men's basketball team|Eastern Washington]] in the [[2015 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2015 NCAA tournament]], and he made his greatest contributions to the team over the next two seasons. He finished his career having played in 94 games, starting 38 of them, shooting 53.4 percent from the field and averaging 4.0 points and 3.4 rebounds per game.<ref>[https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/players/bradley-hayes-1.html sports-reference.com Bradley Hayes College stats Retrieved July 20, 2018]</ref> Cameron appeared in 104 games in his four years at Georgetown, starting 18 of them, and finished his college career with a 37.4 shooting percentage from the field overall and 32.6 percent from three-point range, averaging 3.4 points and 1.3 rebounds per game.<ref>[https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/players/reggie-cameron-1.html sports-reference.com Reggie Cameron College stats Retrieved July 20, 2018]</ref>

At the end of the season, and with a new coach, the Hoyas faced an uncertain future. The failure of most of John Thompson III's recent recruiting efforts and the loss of the team's top scorers left Georgetown with what ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' writer [[Pete Thamel]] described as a "program [that] is already buzz-less, lacking an on-court identity," and with "a roster so devoid of talent it would make 1980s Hoyas weep."<ref name=thamel20170403/> Ewing was untested as a head coach and lacked familiarity with modern college basketball,<ref name=thamel20170403/> and his hiring was viewed as a great gamble that had a high potential payoff if he quickly learned how to navigate the complexities of college recruiting and player development.<ref name=thamel20170403/> As one of his first steps, Ewing attempted to re-recruit Tremont Waters, but Waters ultimately spurned his efforts, and in June he committed to [[LSU Tigers men's basketball|LSU]] instead.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Conway|first=Tyler|title=4-Star PG Tremont Waters Commits to LSU After Release from Georgetown|url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2700285-4-star-pg-tremont-waters-commits-to-lsu-after-release-from-georgetown|access-date=2022-10-16|website=Bleacher Report|language=en}}</ref> Georgetown's program was in decline, and Waters's decision demonstrated how little attraction it held for nationally prominent recruits, The Hoyas were relying on Ewing to lay a foundation for it to return to national greatness.<ref name=thamel20170403/>
